newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung urges democrat Lee not to mislead U.S.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung urges democrat Lee not to mislead U.S.

text.p: Hong Kong's future chief Tung Chee-hwa on Friday criticised democracy movement leader Martin Lee, urging him not to mislead U.S. President Bill Clinton about the territory as China prepares to take over in July.

Tung said he was disappointed with Lee, who is on a tour of North America where he has warned about China's plans to curb political rights and install a provisional legislature to replace the elected lawmaking body.
"I hope Mr Lee will be speaking really, what is really happening in Hong Kong and present a real picture," Tung told a news conference.
"So far, I have to tell you, I am disappointed," Tung said.
Lee and Clinton were meeting on Friday in Washington.
Tung, who this week called off a pre-handover visit to the United States on the grounds that he was too busy, said he hoped to make the trip next year.
"But I think even if I do not go, the truth will eventually speak for itself. My American friends will see that Hong Kong is fine, Hong Kong will be fine," he said.

Tung urged the territory's departing colonial government to change heart and allow the provisional legislature to draw up a law on who will have the right of abode in Hong Kong after it returns to Chinese control.
The colonial government insists that such a law should not be made by the interim body before the handover.
Tung said he would continue talks with the government on the issue, but would at the same time press ahead with a draft bill for the provisional legislature.
He defended plans to amend civil rights laws, with limits on demonstrations and foreign funding of political groups.
"This law is not to stifle freedom. We want freedom to be here. It will be here," he said, adding that the curbs were not directed at specific parties or individuals.
He reiterated that the amended laws as proposed were less restrictive than those in many other cities in the world, including in North America and Asia.
But Hong Hong's present administration rejected the claim on Friday night.
"It is clear that the procedures governing public processions in the U.K., the U.S. and Canada are considerably less restrictive than those proposed (by Tung)," a government statement said.

While the government opposes the proposals, top civil servant Anson Chan, who will remain in her post under Tung's administration, sought to quell fears over curtailment to civil liberties, noting the public was being consulted.
"There is no question of a severe dilution of individual freedoms," Chan, the Chief Secretary, told a business assembly.
Hong Kong democrats said there was no sign that Tung would retreat from the planned curbs, despite assurances he has given to ease fears of repression.
On Friday, Chan also urged the U.S. to renew China's special trading privileges and said Hong Kong's handover should not be linked to the issue.
Earlier on Thursday, Lee was in Canada, which has a big Hong Kong emigrant community. He criticised Canada's decision not to back a U.N. resolution condemning China's human rights record.
Lu Ping, China's top policymaker for Hong Kong, also began a speaking tour in Vancouver to woo support.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China as a quasi-autonomous region at midnight on June 30 under a treaty allowing its capitalist system to continue for 50 years.
